title: Dhyana: What Patanjali Actually Meant
description: Patanjali defined meditation as unbroken attention and assumed the flow would break. Returning is the practice.
content:
Patanjali defined meditation in the Yoga Sutras with a precision that most modern meditation instruction does not inherit. Dhyana, he wrote, is an unbroken flow of attention toward its object. Not emptiness. Not bliss. Not silence. Unbroken attention. A sustained connection between the observer and the observed.

He also defined what happens when that flow breaks, which he assumed it would. He called the interruption vritti: a fluctuation of the mind, a thought arising, attention moving away. This was not, in Patanjali's view, failure. It was the material you were working with. The practice of meditation was not the achievement of stillness. It was the act of noticing the fluctuation and returning. That act of noticing and returning is the practice. The repetition of that act, over time, is what builds the capacity.

You sat down. Your mind went to your to-do list. You decided you're not someone who can meditate. Patanjali would have said: you just described the first five minutes of every meditation session that has ever occurred. What you did isn't evidence that you can't meditate. It's evidence that your mind is doing what minds do. The question is what you do when you notice it.

The modern expectation that a successful meditation session feels quiet, peaceful, and empty has no basis in classical instruction. Patanjali described a gradient of concentration states (dharana, dhyana, samadhi) that develop over years of consistent practice. The early stages are characterized by exactly the experience you're having: attention to an object, distraction, return. Attention, distraction, return. This is what training looks like. A weightlifter doing a set is not failing when the weight resists. Resistance is the training.

The instruction is simpler than most people receive.

Pick one object for the duration of the session. Your breath. A mantra. A point in the body. One object. When you notice you've left it and you will return. Do not assess the session by how many times you left. Assess it only by whether you returned. Returning is the action. Everything else is context.

Patanjali also described something he called abhyasa and vairagya as the paired requirements for the practice. Abhyasa is consistent practice over a long time, without interruption, approached with care. Vairagya is non-attachment to the results of practice. These two together. Consistent effort without grasping at particular outcomes. You sit. You practice. You notice. You return. You do not evaluate whether today was better than yesterday. You show up tomorrow.

The mistake most people make is irregular long sessions followed by weeks of nothing. What the research and Patanjali supports is short daily practice. Ten minutes every morning, consistently, for three months, produces measurable changes in sustained attention, stress reactivity, and emotional regulation. A ninety-minute session once a week does not. The nervous system adapts to what it does repeatedly. Give it daily repetition.

You don't have a meditation problem. You had a wrong definition of what the practice is. Now you have the right one. Sit down tomorrow morning. Breathe. When the mind goes somewhere else, return. That's it. That's the whole instruction. Patanjali wrote it in three words two thousand years ago. It still holds.
